This game is shallow and very restrictive. 
You can't do anything with your rig.
You can't reply to mails during a mission (yeah, it's useless but I expected some minor rôle play elements).

This game will make you feel like the hacking gods you see in any cheesy hacker movie.  I like that, for the most part, the Linux commands there in their familiar form. It's also very cool to see the different backstories you can find when you take time to dig around every computer.  Also, the Bash.org tidbits in there are always a laugh.  Taking the time to go through every file on every server I could get my hands on gave me a final play through time between 4 and 5 hours, and I really feel like I got my money's worth out of it.  You'll feel stressed like a mofo as you watch the trace counting down while you're just waiting for PortHack to free up memory so you can run TraceKill. You'll feel like a detective tracing encrypted packet headers around a network trying to find a vulnerability, and you'll feel like a total boss by the time you've won.

Hacknet is an excellent hacking game, even for those who are already familiar with linux command line interfaces IRL. It is also interesting for those who want to learn about computer networks and hacking as it is somewhat quite realistic although simple on certain aspects. The only downside is that it can be sometimes a bit repetitive, but in counterpart it is very fascinating due to the captivating story that motivates you to move forward to know the final ending. It has some secrets and hidden achievements that are very pleasant to unlock, and also tons of stupid IRC logs on the computers that you hack that are very fun to read. It took me 12h to complete the game at 100% and it was a memorable experience. Hi5 to my brother who offered it for my bday.

I went in expecting the game to be mediocre at best, but found myself greatly enjoying every minute of it. The gameplay isn't necessarily challenging in any respect, but putting together the puzzles in the world through context, and getting revenge on the occasional attack is greatly enjoyable.

Fair warning, the game isn't exactly immune to bugs, I've had a quest not complete that blocked my progress that I had to work around by hacking into the gamesave file, a bit ironic, and achievements seem to be a bit tempermental.

Outside of that though, especially for the price, I would definately recommend it. The premise of a Metasploit OS on steroids certainly makes for an interesting concept and the developer did a great job on its execution. I greatly look forward to what they come out with next.

Hacknet is such a unique experience - it is designed well, and continues to throw the player curveballs. Often, the game is able to do much more with such a simple interface than you can imagine. The game did a good job of capturing my imagination, despite the vast majority of the game looking like an MS Dos prompt. You may steal files from other servers, delete files that were acquired illegally, alter school records or those of death row inmates, and (in what was the highlight of the game to me) even hack a pacemaker. The only issue I had with the game was when one particular server would not accept a password that I had right in front of me. The password explicitly referenced the server I was attempting to access, but something was lost in my ability to transcribe it. An N looked like an M, and the numbers 1 and 2 appeared to be of different heights. The game doesn't allow you to copy and paste, and I could never quite figure out what the password was supposed to be. I ended up looking up a separate password that I needed (that I was to find on the first server in question) to continue the game. Otherwise, the game is quite clever, and at times requires some lateral thinking. If you want a unique gaming experience, you should give it a try.

This game is definitely fun to play, even though it looks fairly basic at first, and probably won't last you more than 8-15 hours (depending on whether you want to do one playthrough or more).

Your role is that of... yourself, hacker extraordinaire—or something, because in the beginning, your character is probably just fiddling around with their computer. Until they receive an e-mail from Bit, late hacker who's posthumously trying to accomplish what they couldn't do when alive. Armed with a couple of commands and utilities, it's time to jump into the game, a game that may turn out to be bigger than you'd think.

Through a series of e-mails and missions, you get introduced gradually to other hackers, become part of hacking groups, and discover what's hiding behind the Bit case. The game is fairly straightforward in that regard (get a mission, hack ports, hack your way in, steal/delete data, delete logs, disconnect), and getting the tools you need isn't hard, however most of the computers you discover along the way also contain other files you can read, such as IRC logs, and part of the fun I had came from exploring. You also have to make a few choices that may affect which missions are available to you—for instance, accepting missions from another hacker will prevent you from taking another hacker's contracts—as well as a couple of other choices about more ethically-challenged assignments.

The interface is simple enough, in a "minimalist OS" way, with a few animations when running hacking utilities; I quite liked that, as seeing more "Holywood hacking animations" wouldn't have been very believable (but not displaying anything would, on the other hand, be a bit boring). I didn't really like the window with nodes representing all the computers you could access, though: it was nice in the beginning, then became seriously cluttered (in the end, I'd just type the IP addresses directly in the terminal, it was faster).

Interestingly, if you've never worked with Unix-based workstations, or Linux, this can actually be a nice little introduction to that kind of OS. Very basic, obviously, with commands that don't even need any arguments; still, since a lot of what you have to do in game is terminal-based, be ready to type fast and work with commands much more than with just clicking on buttons (being used to TABbing my way both in bash and on IOS, I was totally fine with that, and most often I would be faster this way). Getting the hang of this isn't very difficult, and even if you know nothing to running commands, the game will easily make you feel like you do.

Sounds and music: mostly music, with one voiceover at a given point, and alerts when you're getting traced. At first, I feared the audio tracks would become repetitive; in the long run, they fit pretty well, with appropriate change of tracks when you get into a new hacking group or attempt a new kind of operation, and provided good background music without being intrusive.

Problems I noticed: the game runs in full-screen and would crash when I alt-tabbed out of it. Not sure if it's just my computer, or systematic. It didn't detract from my enjoyment, so I admit I didn't pay much attention (and didn't exactly *have to* alt-tab out of it anyway, since the immersion is much better if you don't).

Awaiting the next DLC now? I also wouldn't mind multiplayer possibilities, like hacking each other, or having to form alliances. That would be fun as well.

Conclusion: Recommended.
